questions.prompt_markup: A histogram with bins of width 1 has counts 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 2, so it looks jagged. Why might bins of width 2 help?

choices.text: Wider bins always make a distribution look symmetric.
Wider bins change the data values, so the shape becomes smoother.
Wider bins add values to the empty bins, so no bin is 0.
Wider bins group nearby values, so the overall shape is easier to see.

questions.correct_answer: Wider bins group nearby values, so the overall shape is easier to see.

choices.text: Yes: halve each count, because each narrower bin is half as wide.
Yes: keep the same counts, because the data have not changed.
No: each count could be split between the two narrower bins in many ways.
No: a histogram with bins of width 10 cannot be redrawn at all.

questions.correct_answer: No: each count could be split between the two narrower bins in many ways.
questions.grading_note: Combining bins loses information that cannot be recovered. Halving assumes an even split; the others are false.
